      9. Ordinary generating functions: ordered arrangements, compositions, and recurrences#

      Suppose a staircase may be climbed using steps of several allowed heights. If we use exactly four steps, then the order of the four heights matters: the sequence describes a different climb from . If the number of steps is not fixed, we must also account for every possible sequence length. Ordinary generating functions can record both the total height and the number of steps, while multiplication records the choices made in successive positions.

      The same construction leads to compositions of an integer. Changing from an ordered list of parts to an unordered collection of parts leads instead to integer partitions and a different generating function. These examples also produce recurrences: a climb can be classified by its final step, and a recursive object can be classified by the smaller objects attached to its root.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • Use the substitutions and to impose divisibility and remainder conditions on exponents.

      • Construct the OGF for ordered arrangements of exactly objects by first assigning a separate variable to each position.

      • Interpret the composition as replacing each position of an outer arrangement by an inner object.

      • Count climbs of a prescribed height with either a fixed or unrestricted number of allowed steps.

      • Distinguish integer compositions from integer partitions and construct their generating functions.

      • Derive Fibonacci and Catalan recurrences from combinatorial decompositions and translate those recurrences into OGF equations.

      Example 2 (Parity conditions in a product)#

      A bag contains red, blue, and green tokens of each color in unlimited supply. How many selections of tokens use an even number of red tokens, an odd number of blue tokens, and any number of green tokens?

      The three color counts are independent and order does not matter. Their OGFs are, respectively, Therefore the required number is Each selected collection contributes once: its red, blue, and green counts choose one term from each of the three factors, and the exponents add to the total number of tokens.

      9.2 A fixed number of positions in an ordered arrangement#

      Products have represented independent choices throughout this unit. For an ordered arrangement, the factors represent successive positions. Keeping a different variable for each position makes this interpretation visible before we combine the recorded sizes.

      Suppose that one step may have a height in a set of positive integers. For the moment, consider an arrangement of exactly three steps. Use for the first position, for the second, and for the third. The product contains the monomial for the ordered sequence . Because the variables retain the position numbers, the monomial is different from .

      9.3 Substitution as replacement of ordered positions#

      The preceding construction can be written as a substitution of one generating function into another. Let count outer arrangements with positions, and let count the objects that may fill one position. The variables are deliberately different: counts unfilled positions in the outer arrangement, while counts the size contributed by a filling object.

      An outer arrangement with exactly ordered positions has weight . Replacing each of those positions independently by a -object changes that weight to If there are possible outer arrangements of length , their total contribution is . Summing over all gives Thus the algebraic substitution represents a combinatorial replacement: every outer position is filled by one inner object.

      Proposition 5 (OGF substitution rule)#

      Let count outer arrangements by their number of positions. Let count the allowed fillings of one position by size. If the positions of each outer arrangement are distinct, and each position is filled independently, then counts the resulting objects by total size.

      For an ordered sequence there is one outer arrangement of every length, so Substitution gives The term counts sequences of exactly objects. The constant term counts the empty sequence, which has length and total size zero.

      9.5 Partitions of an integer#

      Definition 10 (Partition)#

      A partition of a positive integer is an unordered collection of positive integers whose sum is . We write the parts in weakly decreasing order so that each partition has one representation.

      The partitions and are therefore the same partition of , even though and are different compositions. To construct a partition, choose a nonnegative number of parts of size , a nonnegative number of parts of size , and so on. The choices for parts of size have OGF The choices for different part sizes are independent, so their product is the partition generating function.

      9.6 Recurrences from the final step#

      A recurrence relation defines terms of a sequence using earlier terms. A recurrence must be accompanied by initial conditions, since the rule alone generally describes many sequences.

      Let be the number of ordered climbs of height using step heights in a fixed set of positive integers. Count the empty climb by , and set for . Every nonempty climb has a unique final step of some height . Removing that final step leaves a climb of height . Conversely, appending an -step to a climb of height produces a unique climb of height whose final step has height . The classes for distinct final-step heights are disjoint, so

      The OGF gives the same equation. If , then ordered climbs have OGF Equivalently, The term represents the empty climb. In , the factor chooses a distinguished final step and chooses the shorter climb that precedes it. Comparing coefficients gives the recurrence above.

      9.6.2 Catalan numbers from a split into two smaller objects#

      The Catalan recurrence arises from a different decomposition. Let count full rooted binary trees with internal vertices, and let count the tree consisting of a single leaf. In a nontrivial tree, the root is an internal vertex with a left subtree and a right subtree. If the left subtree has internal vertices, the right subtree must have internal vertices. The integer may range from to .

      For a fixed , there are choices for the left subtree and choices for the right subtree. The product rule and then the sum rule give Starting from , this recurrence gives

      Let The Cauchy product records an ordered pair consisting of a left and a right subtree. Multiplication by records the new internal root. Including the size-zero tree gives the OGF equation The coefficient of in is so the generating-function equation and the Catalan recurrence express the same root decomposition. Solving this quadratic equation for and extracting a closed formula are later steps; the recurrence already computes each term from earlier ones.

      9.7 Ordered and unordered constructions compared#

      The form of a generating function depends on what constitutes one object.

      • Exactly ordered parts chosen from are counted by .

      • Any finite ordered sequence of such parts is counted by .

      • Compositions use ordered positive parts, so their OGF is built from powers of .

      • Partitions use a multiplicity for every possible part size, so their OGF is the product .

      • A recurrence results when every nonempty object has a unique decomposition into smaller objects, as in the final-step decomposition or the root decomposition of a binary tree.

      Before selecting a formula, decide whether positions are ordered, what one exponent measures, and whether the number of parts is fixed. Those choices determine whether the construction requires a power, a geometric series of powers, or a product indexed by allowable part sizes.
